parts.title: My grandfather, the magician
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
My grandfather was a magician for forty years, and when I was small, I thought that he really had magic powers. He could make coins appear from my ears and turn a scarf into a flower. I begged him to teach me his secrets, but he always smiled and said, "A magician never tells."

On my twelfth birthday, he finally gave me a small black box. Inside were a pack of cards, three coloured balls and a note that said, "Practise every day for a year, and then ask me again." I thought that it was a joke, but I did what he said.

It was much harder than I expected. For months, I dropped the balls and forgot the order of the cards. Slowly, though, my hands learned what to do. After a year, I showed him my first trick. He watched very carefully, and then he clapped. "Not bad," he said, "but you looked at your hands. Never look at the secret. Look at the audience."

That was the best lesson of all. Now I perform at parties, and I always keep my eyes on the faces in front of me. Last week, a child asked me how I did a trick, and I smiled and said, "A magician never tells."

options: Magic was too hard to learn
questions.explanation: She says she thought that he really had magic powers.

options: A hat, a long cape and a wand

questions.explanation: He said that she looked at her hands.

parts.title: Why magic works
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Magic tricks seem impossible, but they all use simple ideas. [1] A good magician knows how to use these ideas without anyone noticing.

The most important idea is attention. Our brains can only follow one thing at a time. [2] While you watch the right hand, the left hand quietly does the secret work.

Another idea is that people believe what they expect to see. [3] If a magician shows you an empty box, you will usually think that it is empty, even if you did not check.

Magicians also practise their words. [4] A friendly joke or a story can make the audience look away at exactly the right moment.

For this reason, many scientists now study magic. [5] They want to learn how the human brain decides what is real.
sentences: Most magicians begin to perform when they are very young.
The tricks give them a safe way to test how people think.
Magicians use this by asking you to look at something exciting.
He never explains how they are done.
Our brains often fill in the parts that we cannot see.
The things they say are as important as the things they do.
None of them needs special powers, only skill and planning.
Some magicians use animals, such as rabbits and doves, in their shows.

gaps.explanation: The tricks use simple ideas and need no special powers; the next sentence says a good magician uses these ideas.
The brain follows one thing at a time, so magicians ask you to look at something exciting.
The brain fills in what it cannot see; the next sentence gives the empty box example.
Magicians practise their words, which are as important as their actions; the next sentence gives a joke or story.
The tricks help scientists test how people think; the next sentence says what they want to learn.

parts.title: Learning a magic trick
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: A simple trick that you can learn in ten minutes uses only a coin and a scarf. [1] first, practise in front of a mirror. This will help you see what your audience sees. Do not tell anyone how the trick works, [2] they will not be impressed. When you perform, speak in a clear voice and smile. If you make a mistake, do not stop. Often, the audience will not notice, as [3] as you stay calm. After a few weeks, you will be able to do the trick without [4] at your hands. Many people also like to wear a special hat, [5] makes the show more fun. And remember, practice is [6] key to success.

gaps.explanation: At first is a fixed phrase meaning in the beginning.
Or means if you tell them, they will not be impressed.
As long as means on condition that.
After without we use the -ing form: without looking at your hands.
Which refers to the whole idea of wearing a special hat.
The key to success is a fixed phrase.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Was the magic show good, Eli? I heard there was a big trick with a car.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: They advertised it, but it was cancelled because of the rain. Maybe next week. They did the rope trick instead, but I’ve seen it ten times, and it’s not as exciting as it sounds.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: So was it boring?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Not at all. At the end the magician took off his hat, shook it, and a white bird flew out of it. Everyone screamed, even the grown-ups.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Wow. I wish I had gone.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Come with me next time.

options: Pulled a bird from a hat
Cut a long rope in half
question.explanation: The car trick was cancelled and the rope trick was an old one; the best moment was when a white bird flew out of his hat.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Your brother says that you can do fifteen magic tricks, Ben. Is that true?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: No, that’s what I’d like. I learned two last year, but I’ve forgotten how they work. Now I have practised one for each finger on my hand, and they’re quite good. I’m learning a new one, but it isn’t ready.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Impressive! You must be proud. Will you show me?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Tomorrow, after school, in the garden. I need to find my cards first, and my sister has hidden them again.

question.prompt: How many tricks can the boy do?
question.explanation: Fifteen is only what he would like and two were last year’s tricks; he has practised one for each finger of his hand, so five.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Hi Paula, it’s Tom. You asked me where to buy the magic set for Max. I thought the toy shop was next to the cinema, because I remember a window with teddy bears, but that’s a sweet shop. Someone told me it’s behind the library, but I walked there and found only a car park. In the end, I asked a friendly taxi driver, and he told me it’s on the other side of the road from the bank, between the post office and the flower shop. It closes at half past five, so go after your lesson. Call me if you need anything. Bye!

question.explanation: The cinema was a mistake and the library only has a car park; the taxi driver said that it is across the road from the bank.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Did you go to the magic show on Saturday? My cousin said everyone was laughing.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Yes! At the start a child shouted "I can see the rabbit!" so loudly that we all jumped, but the magician only smiled.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Was it when the lights went out?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: No, that was part of the trick, and it was a little scary. The biggest laugh came when he dropped his wand. It fell right on his toes, and he hopped around on one leg, saying, "That wasn’t in the plan!"

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Ha! I wish I had seen that.

question.explanation: The shouting child made people jump and the lights going out was part of the trick; the laughter came when the wand fell on his toes.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Can you tell me when the magic show finishes? My son needs to get the train at twenty past five.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Well, the ticket says four o’clock, but that’s when the interval starts. The show began at three and it lasts one hour and forty minutes.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Oh, I see. So we have time to walk to the station.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Yes, plenty of time. But don’t wait at the door too long, because the crowd is big.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Thanks, I’ll tell my son. He gets nervous when he is late for anything.

question.explanation: Four o’clock is the interval and twenty past five is the train; three o’clock plus one hour and forty minutes gives twenty to five.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: What did you think of the coin trick, Jack? It was so confusing.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Honestly, it was easy. I watched his left hand all the time, and he passed the coin to his sleeve. I told my brother and he didn’t believe me until the end.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Really? I thought you’d be confused. Last time you didn’t get the card trick.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: That’s true. But this time I knew exactly what he was doing. And I love coins, I collect them, so I looked at that one very carefully.

question.prompt: What does the boy say about the trick?
question.explanation: He did not understand the card trick last time, and he collects coins; this time he watched the left hand and saw the coin go to the sleeve.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Is it true that your dad will be the magician at your birthday party, Lily?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I asked him, but he can’t do magic. He can only make coffee disappear. Then I asked my teacher, and Mr Brown said yes, but he’s busy that day. So my brother Max will do it. He’s been learning tricks for months.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: That sounds great. Is he good?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: He’s getting better. He needs a costume though.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I have a hat and a black cape you can borrow. It was my grandfather’s.

question.explanation: Her dad cannot do magic and the teacher is busy, so her brother Max, who has been learning tricks, will do it.

turns.speaker: a

turns.speaker: b

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Yes. You could wait until the prices go down in January, if you prefer.

turns.text: Of course.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Do you think magic is real, Noah? My sister says that some people have special powers.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: No way. People say that it comes from ancient times, and yes, it’s very old, but that doesn’t make it real. It’s all clever tricks.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: But it can be boring too, can’t it? Some shows are really slow.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Not for me. I love watching the hands and the mirrors and trying to find the secret. That’s what makes it exciting.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I prefer to believe in the magic.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Fine, but I know it’s cleverness.

question.prompt: What does Noah think about magic?
options: It is real and very old
It is made of clever tricks
question.explanation: He agrees it is very old but not real, and he finds it exciting rather than slow; for him it is all clever tricks.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Class, next Friday a magician is coming to our school. He has performed in many countries, and I think you will enjoy it.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Cool! Will he teach us a trick?

turns.speaker: a

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Great, I like science more than magic. Is there a test afterwards?

turns.speaker: a

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Even better. I’m excited. Can we ask him questions at the end, Miss?

turns.speaker: a

options: Pleased because he likes the science part
Worried because there is a test

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Hello, is that Mr Lopez, the magician? I saw your website.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Yes, speaking. How can I help?

turns.speaker: a

turns.speaker: b

turns.speaker: a

parts.title: A talk at a magic club
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: leader
turns.text: Welcome to the Young Magicians’ Club. I am Sasha, and I have been running this club for six years. I have been doing magic for much longer, about twenty years, but it was only six years ago that I opened this club in the town hall. We meet every Tuesday at half past six. We used to meet on Thursdays, but the room was busy with the dance class. Please come on time, because we start with a short game. Now, money. One session costs four pounds. If you want to join for the whole term, it is thirty pounds. Visitors pay five pounds, but only for the first time, and then they can become members. You pay at the desk by the door, and I will give you a small ticket as a receipt, so please keep it safe. Tonight, we have a lot to do. I’d like to show you three card tricks. Some of you asked for coin tricks, and we will do those next week, but tonight it is all about cards. Bring your own pack, or borrow one of mine. They are old, but they work very well, and nobody will mind if a corner is bent. Next, our big event. Every year we show our magic to the parents. This year’s show is on the fourteenth of December, in the main hall. The dress rehearsal is two days before that, on the twelfth, so please write both dates down. You don’t need a costume, but a hat is welcome. Finally, each member must prepare one trick for the show. It can be a short, simple one, and it can be one from the club or a trick you made up. You don’t have to find an assistant, because we have helpers. Thank you, and let’s get started.

gaps.explanation: She opened the club six years ago; twenty years is how long she has done magic.
They meet on Tuesday; Thursday was the old day.
One session costs four pounds; five is the price for visitors and thirty is for the term.

gaps.prompt: Tonight's lesson is about three ___ tricks
gaps.explanation: Tonight is about card tricks; coin tricks come next week.

gaps.prompt: The show for the parents is on the ___ of December
gaps.explanation: The show is on the fourteenth; the twelfth is the dress rehearsal.

gaps.prompt: For the show, each member must prepare a short ___
gaps.explanation: Each member prepares one trick; they do not need an assistant or a costume.

parts.title: An interview with a young magician
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Gage, you’re only sixteen and you’re already a professional magician. How did you start?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: When I was seven, I saw a magician at my school, and I thought it was good, but I didn’t think about it much afterwards. A film about magic was on TV, too, and I liked it, but that’s not it. What really began it all was a present from my grandmother: an old book of card tricks. I read it under the blankets every night with a torch, and my mum thought I was reading for school, so she never complained. After three months I could do ten tricks.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: When do you practise?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Not after dinner, because I’m too tired and I make silly mistakes. I’d like to practise on Sundays only, but with exams it’s impossible. So I get up an hour early, before school, when the house is quiet. My hands feel fresh and I can concentrate.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Has a trick ever gone wrong in a show?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Oh yes! Last month, a card fell out of my sleeve in front of two hundred people. I didn’t stop the show, and I didn’t ask anybody to help, because that would have made it worse. I smiled, picked it up, and said, "That’s the card you didn’t choose!" They loved it, and many thought it was planned.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: You also teach. What do you teach children?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Not the secrets of big shows, because I’m not allowed to share those, and I don’t talk about money either. I teach the basics: how to hold the cards, how to move your hands, how to smile when you make a mistake. Small things, but they are the base of everything. When children get these right, they are so proud, and their parents take a lot of photos.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do you prefer young audiences?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Definitely. It’s not about money, because they pay less than adults. And they aren’t quiet at all! If they don’t understand a trick, they shout, "How did you do it?" So I know at once if the trick works. Adults sit silently, and I never know what they think.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What would you like to study at university?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Maths. My teachers say I should do drama, and music is a big part of my shows, but I’m not planning to study either of them. Maths helps me to invent new tricks, because many are based on numbers and patterns. It’s my secret weapon, and I never tell anyone in the audience, because that would be a bit boring. I also read a lot of books about numbers in my free time.
